idiom_name: __add__/__mul__ dunder protocol on a frozen dataclass
implementation_notes: Python's protocol for closed operations is the special-method set: define __add__ (plus __radd__ when scalars or other types may appear on the left) to return a new instance of the same class, so a + b on your Money or Interval type yields that type and reduce/fold work on collections of it. What replaces the classic structure is the dunder protocol plus @dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True), which supplies value equality and blocks attribute assignment, with __post_init__ validating the canonical representation. The dunder form is justified when the operation really is arithmetic; for partial, non-commutative or failure-prone combinations use a named method returning a result/optional type instead of inventing an operator. Note that frozen is emulation, not deep immutability - keep fields immutable or copy on construction.
pitfalls: frozen=True blocks attribute assignment but not mutation of a mutable field (list, dict, set), and it does not make the object hashable if a field is unhashable - the value semantics the pattern assumes must be maintained by hand.

Returning NotImplemented (rather than raising) is the required protocol when an operand type is unsupported; raising TypeError directly breaks Python's reflected-operation dispatch and prevents other classes from handling the operation.
sum() starts from the integer 0, so without __radd__ a fold over Money fails; likewise __rmul__ is needed for 2 * money.
int is unbounded but float and Decimal semantics differ: mixing them into Money arithmetic reintroduces rounding, so keep integer minor units (or Decimal) as the single canonical representation.
